messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jamal is a 23-year-old African American urban planner who has been struggling with the aftermath of an assault that occurred several months ago. Jamal was walking home late one night when he encountered a group of individuals who surrounded him and attacked him violently. The attack left him with significant physical injuries, but it was the psychological impact that continued to haunt him. Jamal’s traumatic experience is deeply etched in his mind as vivid snapshots — moments frozen in time like still frames from a movie. One such moment involves the smell of alcohol on one attacker’s breath, another is the sight of objects being thrown, and yet another is the anger expressed by those who attacked him. These triggers have become potent reminders of that night, causing Jamal to jump or startle at any sudden sound or movement nearby, even when he knows he is in a safe environment. Whenever these triggers occur, Jamal finds himself overwhelmed with emotion, often unable to find words to express what he feels. His memories are so intense that they stop him in his tracks, forcing him to retreat into a cocoon of self-blame and rumination. He dwells on what he could have done differently or if he had acted more decisively, perhaps the attack would not have happened. The trauma has also led Jamal to adopt maladaptive strategies as coping mechanisms. To distract himself from these overwhelming memories and emotions, he turns to gambling. The thrill of gambling provides a temporary escape, but it only serves to exacerbate his feelings of helplessness and institutional failure. Jamal is certain that the police let him down by failing to protect him properly — this belief has solidified over time, leading him to avoid any situations where there might be confrontation or disagreement. Jamal’s sense of low coping ability has worsened as a result of these repeated maladaptive strategies. He feels he cannot deal with even minor upsets and is increasingly convinced that bad things will continue to happen to him. These negative appraisals are reinforced every time he encounters a trigger, further deepening his reliance on self-blame rumination and gambling. Jamal’s work as an urban planner has not been spared either. He often finds himself avoiding meetings or conversations where conflict might arise. The smell of alcohol from colleagues who occasionally drink during casual office hours also triggers his startle response. This has led to a noticeable decline in his performance at work, as he frequently withdraws into his own thoughts and becomes disengaged. The cycle is self-perpetuating: Jamal’s maladaptive strategies intensify his negative appraisals, which in turn worsen the symptoms of threat and memory disturbance. Each time he gambles or dwells on past mistakes, he finds it even harder to trust that he is safe, leading him to react more intensely when triggered. What finally brought Jamal to seek help was a recent incident where he had a panic attack at work after a colleague expressed anger calmly over a minor disagreement. This episode left him feeling isolated and unable to function effectively in his daily life. Jamal is most afraid of losing control again and being unable to protect himself, but he is also hoping that therapy can provide the tools he needs to manage these overwhelming feelings and regain a sense of safety and trust. In summary, Jamal’s journey has been marked by a complex interplay between triggers, maladaptive strategies, negative appraisals, memory disturbances, and perceived threats. His story underscores the need for comprehensive treatment addressing both his psychological symptoms and their underlying causal connections to improve his quality of life and restore his sense of control and safety.
